title: Week 2 Assessment: Thinking and Communicating
intro: This assessment tests how you think and communicate under realistic conditions: evaluating claims, writing clearly, reading emotions, staying calm and acting with confidence. Part A uses auto-graded questions from lessons you completed. Part B has a decision scenario, a role-play and a short writing task.

items.prompt: A teammate says: "Everyone knows that this framework is the best. Only beginners disagree." You have doubts about it for your project. What is the best response?

options.feedback: Agreeing silently leaves your doubts unexamined.

options.text: Ask what evidence supports it for this project and share one specific concern calmly.
options.feedback: It tests the claim and respects the person.
This attacks the person, not the claim.

items.why: Critical thinking asks for evidence while emotional intelligence keeps the tone respectful.

items.setup: You disagree with a classmate's plan during a group project meeting. They sound frustrated when you raise a concern.

turns.they: I think my plan is fine. Why are you objecting now?

options.text: You always do this and it is annoying.
options.reply: Forget it, do whatever you want.

options.text: I can hear you are frustrated. I like the structure; my concern is the deadline in week three. Can we check it together?
options.feedback: It acknowledges emotion, names a specific issue and invites collaboration.
options.reply: Okay, show me where the issue is.

options.feedback: Giving in quickly avoids the issue and may cost later.

turns.they: How could the deadline be a problem?

options.feedback: A feeling without facts is weak.

options.text: The testing task is after the submission date in the schedule. Moving testing one week earlier would fix it.
options.feedback: Concrete fact plus a proposed solution.

turns.they: Can you update the plan and send it?

options.text: Yes, I will send the updated plan by tonight at 8 pm.
Why do I always have to do the work?

items.why: Acknowledge feelings, name concrete issues and make specific commitments.

items.prompt: Write a short, clear email (about 100 words) to a senior asking for one day's extension on a task because a dependency has not been delivered. Include facts, impact, a proposed new date and a polite close.

descriptors.3: Clear subject and request at the start.
Specific new date and professional tone.

items.modelAnswer: Subject: Request for one-day extension on report task. Hello Mr Verma, I am writing to request one extra day on the sales report. The data file from the finance team arrived at 4 pm today instead of yesterday, so I could start the analysis only now. I propose to submit by 12 noon on Thursday instead of Wednesday evening. I will share a draft of sections one and two by tomorrow 3 pm so you can review them early. Thank you for understanding. Regards, Deepak.
items.guidance: Strong emails state the request first, give the specific reason with facts, propose a concrete new date and keep a polite professional tone. Avoid excuses or blame.
